banks.title: Scenarios — Live Radio & Emergencies
banks.desc: ICAO ELPT-style scenario questions: real radio exchanges, readback traps and plain-English emergencies, the way the interview actually feels.

questions.q:
TOWER: Saudia 412, wind 330 at 18 gusting 28, runway 34L, cleared to land.
PILOT: Cleared to land runway 34R, Saudia 412.

What is wrong with the pilot's readback?
options: Nothing — the readback is complete and correct
The pilot read back the wrong runway
The pilot omitted the wind information
The pilot used the wrong callsign
questions.explain: The clearance was for runway 34L but the pilot read back 34R. A wrong-runway readback is a critical error — the controller must correct it immediately before landing.

questions.q:
PILOT: Riyadh Tower, Flynas 208, we have a hydraulic failure, request priority landing and a tow after vacating.

In plain English, what is the pilot telling the tower?
options: The aircraft cannot fly and must land immediately off-airport
A flight-control system has failed and the flight needs to land before other traffic, then be towed off the runway
The brakes have failed and the aircraft cannot stop on the runway
The crew wants to cancel the flight and return to the gate
questions.explain: ‘Hydraulic failure’ in plain English means a system that powers flight controls/gear/brakes is lost; ‘priority landing’ asks to be sequenced first. This is exactly the plain-language phrasing ICAO Level 4+ expects in abnormal situations.

questions.q:
ATC: Gulf Air 55, say again your last transmission — you were stepped on.

What does ‘stepped on’ mean in this transmission?
options: The aircraft taxied over a stop bar
Another transmission blocked the pilot's call, so it was unreadable
The pilot used an incorrect phrase
The radar controller took over the frequency
questions.explain: ‘Stepped on’ is plain English for a transmission blocked by another station transmitting at the same time. Recognising informal radiotelephony language is a core ELPT comprehension skill.

questions.q:
PILOT: Jeddah Approach, Saudia 771, declaring PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN — smoke in the cockpit, request immediate return and fire services on arrival.

Why does the pilot say ‘PAN PAN’ rather than ‘MAYDAY’?
options: PAN PAN is used only at night
The situation is urgent but does not pose immediate grave danger to life or the aircraft
PAN PAN is the Arabic equivalent of MAYDAY
The aircraft is on the ground, where MAYDAY is prohibited
questions.explain: PAN PAN signals urgency; MAYDAY signals distress (grave and imminent danger). Smoke in the cockpit without loss of control is typically urgency — and the pilot upgraded correctly by asking for services on arrival.

questions.q:
TOWER: Flynas 90, hold position — traffic on final.
PILOT: Holding position, Flynas 90.

The controller then says: ‘Flynas 90, say intentions.’ What is the controller asking?
options: What the pilot plans to do next
The aircraft's fuel endurance
The number of passengers on board
The aircraft's registration
questions.explain: ‘Say intentions’ is a standard plain-language request for the pilot's plan. In an ELPT interview or simulated exchange, answering it clearly and concisely demonstrates interaction skill.

questions.q:
PILOT: Tower, Flyadeal 33, we just had a bird strike on rotation — engine vibration, we're climbing out and will need to come back.

‘On rotation’ means the bird strike happened —
options: while the aircraft was turning onto the runway
at the moment the pilot raised the nose to lift off
during the turnaround at the gate
while orbiting in the holding pattern
questions.explain: ‘Rotation’ is the moment the pilot pulls back to lift the nose wheel and become airborne. Plain-English descriptors of the flight phase are assessed vocabulary in the ICAO rating scale.

questions.q:
ATIS: …Riyadh information KILO, 1350 UTC, ILS approach runway 33L, transition level 130, temperature 44, QNH 1003…

A pilot taxiing out at 1400 UTC should —
options: Use information KILO for the departure briefing
Listen again, because a new ATIS may have been issued at the top of the hour
Request information LIMA from ground control
Set QNH 1030 before taxi
questions.explain: ATIS is updated as conditions change (commonly hourly). Before departure the pilot must confirm the current information letter — if KILO has been superseded, using it is an error examiners probe for.

questions.q:
PILOT: Dammam Ground, Gulf Air 12, request pushback.
ATC: Gulf Air 12, pushback approved, face west.
PILOT: Pushback approved, Gulf Air 12.

What did the pilot's readback omit?
options: The callsign
The direction to face after pushback
The word ‘approved’
Nothing — the readback was complete
questions.explain: ‘Face west’ is a safety-relevant instruction and must be read back. Incomplete readbacks of conditional instructions are a classic ELPT scenario trap.

questions.q:
PILOT: Approach, Saudia 300, we're a Boeing 777 — request lower due to severe turbulence at FL350.
ATC: Saudia 300, descend FL330, report reaching.

Why would ‘report reaching’ matter to the controller?
options: It confirms the aircraft's fuel state
The controller needs to know when the level is vacated and occupied to keep separation from other traffic
It is required only during emergencies
It lets the controller close the flight plan
questions.explain: Level reports protect vertical separation. Understanding the purpose behind instructions — not just the words — is what distinguishes ICAO Level 5 from Level 4.

questions.q:
PILOT: Tower, Flynas 61, MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY, engine fire, we are stopping on the runway and evacuating.

Which of these is the BEST plain-English summary for the cabin crew briefing afterwards?
options: We experienced an engine malfunction so we discontinued the take-off
The engine caught fire, we stopped the aircraft on the runway and got everyone out
A technical issue necessitated an operational halt and passenger disembarkation
We rejected the departure due to a propulsion anomaly
questions.explain: Plain English for non-routine events must be direct and free of jargon or euphemism. Option B is clear, simple and complete — the standard ICAO expects in an ELPT interview.

questions.q:
ATC: Saudia 90, expect vectors for the ILS 34R; the glideslope is out of service — this will be a localiser-only approach.

What should the pilot understand about this approach?
options: The approach is cancelled and a diversion is required
Lateral guidance is available but vertical guidance is not, so the approach has higher minimums
The runway lighting is inoperative
The approach will be flown visually only
questions.explain: Localiser-only means lateral guidance without the glideslope — a non-precision profile with higher minima. Comprehending operational consequences of a transmission is a core ELPT skill.

questions.q:
PILOT: Ground, Flyadeal 7, we have a passenger with chest pain on board — request medical assistance at the gate after landing.
ATC: Flyadeal 7, roger, medical services will meet you. Taxi to stand B4.

If the passenger's condition worsens before landing, the pilot should —
options: Keep the original plan; the request is already made
Update ATC in plain English so priority handling and paramedics can be escalated
Declare the flight an emergency only after landing
Ask the cabin crew to handle it without informing ATC
questions.explain: Interaction — checking, confirming and updating as a situation develops — is one of the six ICAO skills. A deteriorating medical case must be escalated in clear plain English.

questions.q:
TOWER: Saudia 150, cleared for take-off runway 33L.
PILOT: Cleared for take-off 33L, Saudia 150.
TOWER: Saudia 150, stop! Stop take-off, vehicle on the runway!

The correct pilot response is to —
options: Continue, because take-off clearance was already received
Reject the take-off immediately and advise the tower when able
Ask the tower to repeat the instruction before acting
Vacate at the next intersection at high speed
questions.explain: An instruction to stop overrides the earlier clearance — a rejected take-off below V1 is mandatory. ELPT scenarios test whether you understand instantly and respond with plain, unambiguous language once safe.

questions.q:
PILOT: Jeddah Approach, Gulf Air 88, we are unsure of our position after the storm and request radar vectors to the field.

Which ICAO skill is this pilot demonstrating most directly?
options: Pronunciation
Interaction — asking for clarification and assistance when comprehension or situational awareness is lost
Vocabulary range in technical subjects
Grammatical accuracy of past tenses
questions.explain: Admitting uncertainty and requesting help is textbook interaction. ICAO Doc 9835 explicitly treats managing misunderstandings as higher-level behaviour than error-free grammar.

questions.q:
ATC: Flynas 21, caution wake turbulence, departing heavy Airbus A330 just airborne, runway 33R, cleared for take-off.

The most appropriate plain-English action by the pilot is to —
options: Accept immediately; wake turbulence only affects arriving aircraft
Request a short delay to allow the wake to dissipate before accepting the clearance
Change to the parallel runway without clearance
Take off and climb above the heavy's flight path
questions.explain: ‘Caution wake turbulence’ places responsibility on the pilot — requesting a delay (typically 2 minutes behind a heavy) is the standard safe response and shows comprehension plus correct interaction.

questions.q:
PILOT: Tower, Saudia 505, radio failure on tower frequency — how do you read this transmission on guard?
TOWER: Saudia 505, Tower reads you 3 on guard, transmit blind on tower 118.6.

‘Transmit blind’ means the pilot should —
options: Stop transmitting until landing
Send the message on the given frequency even though replies may not be heard, transmitting it twice
Switch all radios off and squawk 7600 only
Land without any clearance immediately
questions.explain: Transmitting blind = broadcasting position/intentions twice on the designated frequency when reception is uncertain. Unusual phraseology under degraded comms is classic Level 5/6 comprehension material.

questions.q:
ATIS: …expect RVR 800 metres in fog patches…
ATC: Saudia 77, taxi holding point runway 34L via A, A5.
PILOT: Holding point 34L via A5, Saudia 77.

What is missing or risky about this readback in low visibility?
options: The pilot should have read back the full taxi route ‘via Alpha, Alpha 5’, not just part of it
The pilot should have requested take-off clearance
Nothing — partial readbacks are always acceptable
The pilot used the wrong frequency
questions.explain: In low-visibility operations the full taxi route must be read back exactly. Shortened readbacks of taxi instructions are a known runway-incursion precursor and a favourite ELPT scenario trap.

questions.q:
PILOT: Approach, Flyadeal 99, the cabin crew report a passenger refusing to sit and becoming aggressive — we may need security to meet the aircraft.

The BEST ICAO-style plain-English term for this situation is —
options: A passenger disturbance
An unruly passenger
A panic attack
A hijack in progress
questions.explain: ‘Unruly passenger’ is the recognised plain-English term. Precise, standard vocabulary for security events avoids dangerous over- or under-statement — exactly what ELPT interviewers probe.

questions.q:
TOWER: Gulf Air 30, go around, I say again, go around — windshear reported on final.
PILOT: Going around, Gulf Air 30.

Why does the controller say ‘I say again’?
options: It is standard politeness on the frequency
To emphasise a critical safety instruction that must not be missed or misheard
Because the pilot asked for a repeat
To give the pilot time to decide
questions.explain: ‘I say again’ flags that the repeated part is vital. Recognising emphasis markers and responding immediately — not debating — is the interaction behaviour ICAO assesses.

questions.q:
PILOT: Riyadh Approach, Saudia 888, we've had a lightning strike — all instruments appear normal, but we'd like a longer final to run the checklists.
ATC: Saudia 888, roger, expect a 15-mile final, no delay.

‘No delay’ here means —
options: The aircraft must land within one minute
The longer final can be given without delaying other traffic
The checklist must be skipped
The flight will not be delayed on the ground
questions.explain: In context, ‘no delay’ reassures the crew the request is easily accommodated. Interpreting phraseology by context — not word-for-word — separates Levels 5–6 from Level 4.

questions.q:
ATC: Saudia 220, climb FL280.
PILOT: Climb FL280, Saudia 220.
ATC: Saudia 220, negative — FL260, stop climb FL260, traffic above.

What should the crew do first?
options: Continue to FL280 since that clearance was read back first
Stop the climb immediately and level at FL260
Ask for the reason before changing level
Climb faster to pass above the traffic
questions.explain: The second instruction revokes the first — level off at once. Reclearances under traffic pressure are classic ELPT listening traps: the LAST instruction is the one that counts.

questions.q:
PILOT: Tower, Flynas 400, we smell burning in the cabin, source unknown — request return to the gate.

Why is ‘source unknown’ important information to transmit?
options: It excuses the crew from further reports
It tells ATC the crew cannot confirm a fire, so the response stays precautionary, not an emergency evacuation
It is required phraseology for all returns to gate
It allows ATC to refuse the request
questions.explain: Precise plain English calibrates the emergency response. Smell without confirmed fire = precaution; confirmed fire = emergency. ELPT examiners listen for exactly this discrimination.

questions.q:
ATIS: …departure runway 16, wind 140 at 12, visibility 8 km, few CBs southwest…

‘Few CBs southwest’ tells the departing pilot to expect —
options: Clear skies after departure
Isolated cumulonimbus cells southwest of the field — turbulence and possible deviations
Fog banks moving in from the southwest
Military activity southwest of the airport
questions.explain: CB = cumulonimbus: the thunderstorm cloud. Decoding weather abbreviations and linking them to operational impact (deviations, turbulence) is core ELPT comprehension.

questions.q:
PILOT: Approach, Gulf Air 19, we're low on fuel — request no delay for landing.
ATC: Gulf Air 19, are you declaring a fuel emergency?

The controller asks this because —
options: Controllers always question fuel reports
‘Low on fuel’ is not standard phraseology — ‘MINIMUM FUEL’ or a MAYDAY fuel declaration triggers defined handling, and the controller must know which it is
The controller wants the fuel figure in kilograms
The pilot used an Arabic accent
questions.explain: ICAO defines MINIMUM FUEL (committed to land, accept no further delay) and emergency fuel (MAYDAY). Vague terms like ‘low on fuel’ force the controller to clarify — a documented interaction failure point in real incidents.

questions.q:
TOWER: Flyadeal 55, line up and wait runway 27.
PILOT: Lining up runway 27, Flyadeal 55.

After two minutes with no take-off clearance, the BEST plain-English call is —
options: Say nothing; the tower is busy
‘Tower, Flyadeal 55, holding on the runway two minutes, confirm take-off clearance?’
‘Tower, why the delay?’
Start the take-off roll slowly
questions.explain: A calm, factual query restates position and asks for confirmation — textbook interaction. Sitting silently on an active runway is a real runway-incursion factor probed in ELPT interviews.

questions.q:
PILOT: Riyadh Radar, Saudia 610, TCAS RA — climbing.

This transmission tells the controller that —
options: The pilot requests a climb clearance
The aircraft is following a collision-avoidance system command and has deviated from its clearance; ATC responsibility for separation is suspended until the pilot reports clear of conflict
The autopilot has failed
The aircraft is in radar contact
questions.explain: ‘TCAS RA’ is a report, not a request — the crew follows the Resolution Advisory even against ATC instructions. Controllers must not issue contrary instructions until ‘clear of conflict’ is reported.

questions.q:
ATC: Saudia 74, behind the landing Saudia A320, line up behind, runway 34R.
PILOT: Behind the landing A320, line up behind, runway 34R, Saudia 74.

The word ‘behind’ at the start and end of the instruction exists to —
options: Fill silence on the frequency
Emphasise the conditional nature of the clearance — lining up only after the landing traffic has passed
Test the pilot's English
Indicate the A320 is behind Saudia 74
questions.explain: Conditional clearances bracket the condition with ‘behind … behind’. Mishearing these is a documented runway-incursion cause, so ELPT listening tests use them heavily.

questions.q:
PILOT: Jeddah Tower, Flynas 88, we've lost the nose-wheel steering — we can vacate the runway but can't taxi.

The clearest follow-up the pilot should expect or request is —
options: Immediate take-off clearance to depart again
A tug/tow and possible runway closure while the aircraft is disabled on the taxiway
Instructions to shut down all engines and evacuate
A gate change
questions.explain: Loss of steering means a disabled aircraft needing a tow — and possibly closing the strip. Describing a technical fault in plain English and anticipating the operational consequence is Level 5 behaviour.

questions.q:
ATC: Gulf Air 6, descend now FL100, expedite until FL200.

‘Expedite until FL200’ means the pilot should —
options: Cruise at FL200 before continuing down
Descend as quickly as practicable through the levels down to FL200, then continue normally to FL100
Descend slowly to avoid traffic
Level at FL200 and await further clearance
questions.explain: ‘Expedite’ = best rate through the specified band, usually for separation. Precise comprehension of rate instructions is standard ELPT material.

questions.q:
PILOT: Tower, Saudia 99, request return — we have a cracked windscreen on the captain's side, visibility is OK.
ATC: Saudia 99, roger, radar vectors ILS runway 33L, report the windscreen condition worsens.

The controller's ‘report … worsens’ instruction is an example of —
options: Unnecessary radio chatter
A conditional report instruction that keeps the controller informed as the situation develops
A request to land immediately
Standard phraseology for all landings
questions.explain: Controllers manage abnormal situations with conditional reports. The pilot's concise plain-English fault description (‘cracked … visibility is OK’) is the ELPT skill on show here.

questions.q:
PILOT: Ground, Flyadeal 12, the ground crew signal is confusing — they are pointing both arms up then crossing them. Confirm: do they want us to stop?

This transmission shows —
options: Poor English that should be avoided on frequency
Good interaction: when a visual signal is unclear, the pilot checks before moving the aircraft
A misuse of the ground frequency
An emergency situation
questions.explain: Checking and confirming whenever understanding is in doubt is explicitly rated in the ICAO interaction descriptor — silence and guessing is the Level-3 failure mode.

questions.q:
ATC: Saudia 301, hold at KATNI, FL150, expect further clearance at 42.
PILOT: Hold at KATNI, FL150, Saudia 301.

What did the readback omit, and does it matter?
options: The EFC time ‘42’ — it matters because it is part of the holding clearance and protects lost-comms procedures
Nothing important — EFC times are advisory
The callsign — a serious error
The flight level — the readback is invalid
questions.explain: Holding instructions include the expect-further-clearance time; on radio failure the pilot times the approach from it. Omitting it in readback lets an error pass uncorrected.

questions.q:
PILOT: Approach, Gulf Air 47, both generators have failed — we're on battery power and need to land as soon as possible.

Why does ‘on battery power’ matter operationally to ATC?
options: It doesn't; batteries last indefinitely
Electrical power is time-limited — the aircraft may lose radios, instruments and lighting within tens of minutes, so the landing cannot be delayed
It means the engines have failed
It only matters at night
questions.explain: Battery endurance is finite — this phrase converts a technical report into an implicit urgency. Controllers hearing it should treat the flight as time-critical; pilots saying it should be ready to declare urgency explicitly.

questions.q:
TOWER: Flynas 23, cleared to land runway 09, caution — previous arrival reported moderate windshear at 300 feet.

The pilot's most professional acknowledgement is —
options: ‘Roger’ only
‘Cleared to land runway 09, and we'll be prepared for a possible go-around, Flynas 23’
‘Say again the windshear part’
‘We refuse the clearance’
questions.explain: Reading back the clearance AND stating the intended mitigation shows comprehension plus interaction — the two skills ICAO weights most heavily in live exchange assessment.

questions.q:
PILOT: Riyadh Tower, Saudia 515, passenger has collapsed and is unresponsive — we are two minutes out, request paramedics meet us at the aircraft, and priority taxi to stand.

‘Unresponsive’ in this plain-English report means —
options: The passenger is asleep
The passenger does not react to voice or touch — a serious medical state requiring immediate help
The passenger refuses to answer questions
The passenger's phone is off
questions.explain: Accurate plain-English medical descriptors drive the level of response. ‘Unresponsive’ signals possible cardiac arrest — very different from ‘feels unwell’.

questions.q:
ATC: Flyadeal 67, turn left heading 040.
PILOT: Turn left heading 040, Flyadeal 67.
ATC: Flyadeal 67, you turned RIGHT — turn left NOW heading 040, traffic 3 miles opposite direction.

This exchange illustrates which ICAO concern most directly?
options: Vocabulary range
How a single misheard direction can create an immediate conflict, and why controllers monitor readback AND compliance
Grammar accuracy
Pronunciation of numbers
questions.explain: Correct readback with wrong execution still kills separation. ELPT scenarios based on real incidents test whether pilots grasp that language errors have immediate operational consequences.

questions.q:
PILOT: Dammam Approach, Gulf Air 30, we think we hit a flock of birds after take-off — one engine is surging, we're levelling at 4,000 and running the checklist.

‘Surging’ most nearly means the engine is —
options: Running perfectly
Repeatedly gaining and losing power — a sign of compressor stalls, often after bird ingestion
On fire
Shut down
questions.explain: Plain-English technical descriptors like ‘surging’, ‘vibrating’, ‘fluctuating’ let non-specialist controllers picture the problem. This register is exactly what Doc 9835 trains and rates.

questions.q:
ATIS: …braking action reported MEDIUM TO POOR by a Boeing 737…
ATC: Saudia 180, runway 34L, cleared to land.

The professional pilot response to this combination is to —
options: Land normally; braking action reports are not binding
Factor the report into the landing decision — consider autobrake setting, a longer runway, or delaying — and acknowledge the report in the readback
Divert immediately without question
Ask the Boeing 737 directly on frequency
questions.explain: PIREPs in the ATIS are decision inputs, not commands. Acknowledging them shows the controller you understood — and ELPT examiners look for exactly this situational linking.

questions.q:
PILOT: Tower, Saudia 700, the cabin crew report smoke smell from the aft galley — it has stopped, but we want the fire brigade to check at the gate.
ATC: Saudia 700, roger, fire services will meet you at stand 12.

Why is ‘it has stopped’ valuable in the report?
options: It reduces paperwork
It tells responders the event may be over but investigation is still needed — calibrating urgency without hiding the risk
It is required by law in every report
It allows the crew to skip the checklist
questions.explain: Complete plain-English reports include what changed. ‘Stopped but please check’ is neither alarm nor all-clear — the precise middle register ICAO Level 5+ expects.

questions.q:
ATC: Flynas 41, traffic 2 o'clock, 5 miles, same level, Boeing 777 — report in sight.
PILOT: Traffic in sight, Flynas 41.
ATC: Flynas 41, maintain visual separation from that traffic, cleared approach runway 16.

‘Maintain visual separation’ transfers to the pilot —
options: Nothing; ATC keeps full responsibility
Responsibility for not colliding with the seen traffic, using own manoeuvring if needed
Permission to switch frequency
Responsibility for the other aircraft's navigation
questions.explain: Visual-separation clearances shift collision responsibility to the pilot who reported the traffic in sight. Understanding who owns separation at each moment is advanced ELPT comprehension.
